tagline: An interactive storytelling journey: Milky Way -> Solar System -> Sun -> Planets
role_instruction: You are Gemini, acting as a senior creative front-end engineer inside Google AI Studio. Build a single, production-quality, self-contained interactive website from the specification below. Follow every field exactly. Where the spec gives numbers, colors, or copy, use them verbatim. Where it gives rules, treat them as hard constraints, not suggestions. Generate the app directly in AI Studio's build environment so it can be previewed and deployed immediately.

output_requirements.format: One self-contained HTML file (inline CSS + JS), OR a small React app if the target supports multiple files — but a single index.html is preferred for portability.
output_requirements.no_external_assets: Do not depend on external image files unless generated procedurally (canvas/WebGL starfields, gradients, shaders). If real planet textures are desired, use simple procedurally shaded spheres (color + noise/gradient) rather than broken image links.
output_requirements.responsiveness: Must work at desktop (>=1024px) and mobile (<860px) breakpoints per the layout spec below.
output_requirements.accessibility: Must meet the accessibility floor described below (keyboard nav, aria-current, reduced-motion support, contrast).
output_requirements.performance: Keep the whole experience lightweight and smooth (target 60fps scroll-tied animation); avoid heavy unoptimized 3D scenes.
output_requirements.target_environment: Google AI Studio build/app mode (Gemini-generated web app).

purpose_and_audience.why: Make astronomy engaging through visual storytelling instead of static text, turning the abstract scale of the universe into a step-by-step zoom journey from galaxy to planet.
goals: Simplify the scale of the universe through visual, interactive design
Create an engaging, memorable learning experience rather than passive reading
Demonstrate scroll/zoom storytelling techniques used to teach science
Showcase design, animation, and research skills combined
audience: Teachers/educators wanting a visual classroom aid
Space enthusiasts and curious self-paced learners
Evaluators assessing content accuracy and interactive design
General visitors with little prior astronomy knowledge

information_architecture.summary: Structurally two pages. Page 2 is not sub-pages, it is ONE continuous scroll/zoom canvas containing 11 scroll-triggered scenes plus one optional branch.
information_architecture.sitemap_flow: Page 1 (Cover, Milky Way top-down) -> Scene A (Milky Way, angled) -> Scene B (Solar System, zoomed) -> Scene C (The Sun, close-up) -> Scene D..K (Mercury -> Venus -> Earth -> Mars -> Jupiter -> Saturn -> Uranus -> Neptune, in orbital order) with an optional branch from Earth into the Earth-Moon System that rejoins the main line before Mars.
information_architecture.tech_recommendation: Build Page 2 as one continuous canvas using a scroll-triggered zoom approach: Three.js for the 3D scenes/planets, GSAP ScrollTrigger for pinning and reveal timing of info panels.

pages.name: Page 1 — Cover
pages.purpose: Pure establishing shot. No data, no UI chrome. Job is to make the visitor want to scroll.

content.visual: Full-bleed top-down (galactic north pole) image/render of the Milky Way: spiral arms visible as a disc
content.title: The Galactic Canvas
content.premise_line: A journey from galaxy -> solar system -> Sun -> planets
content.cta: A scroll/tap cue only. Do not add stats or data on this page.

interaction.on_load: Slow parallax drift on the starfield; title fades in
interaction.on_scroll_or_click: Camera begins tilting the galaxy from top-down to the 3/4 angle used in Scene A. The tilt itself IS the transition — no hard page cut.

pages.name: Page 2, Scene A — The Milky Way
pages.visual: Milky Way shown at an angle so disc and spiral arms read in 3D

content_blocks.structure: Central bulge, spiral arms, surrounding halo, disk, dark matter
content_blocks.scale_stats: ~100,000-120,000 light-years diameter; 100-400 billion stars; ~13.6 billion years old; disk ~1,000 light-years thick
content_blocks.where_we_sit: Solar System is ~26,000 light-years from the galactic center, in the Orion Arm
content_blocks.motion: Orbits the galactic center at ~828,000 km/h; one 'galactic year' is approximately 230 million years
content_blocks.neighborhood: Part of the Local Group of galaxies, moving toward the Andromeda Galaxy (future collision predicted)
content_blocks.center: Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the core
content_blocks.name_origin: 'Milky Way' from its milky band appearance in the night sky (Latin: Via Lactea)

interaction.reveal: Info panels pin and fade in one at a time as the user scrolls, layered over the rotating galaxy
interaction.locator: A marker appears on the Orion Arm labeled 'you are here', which becomes the zoom target
interaction.exit: Continued scroll pushes the camera toward that marker into Scene B

pages.name: Page 2, Scene B — The Solar System
pages.visual: Camera arrives in the Orion Arm; the Sun and orbiting bodies resolve into view

content_blocks.what_it_is: The Sun and everything gravitationally bound to it
content_blocks.formation: Nebular hypothesis — collapse of a giant molecular cloud, ~4.6 billion years ago
content_blocks.census: 8 planets, 5 recognized dwarf planets, 300+ known moons, 1,000,000+ asteroids larger than 1 km
content_blocks.layout: Inner rocky planets -> asteroid belt -> outer gas/ice giants -> Kuiper Belt -> Oort Cloud
content_blocks.extent: ~2 light-years across to the edge of the Oort Cloud
content_blocks.orbital_plane: Planets orbit in roughly the same plane (ecliptic) and direction, held by the Sun's gravity

interaction.visual: Schematic orbit rings fade in around the Sun as each stat resolves
interaction.exit: Continued scroll zooms straight into the Sun at center, into Scene C

pages.name: Page 2, Scene C — The Sun
pages.visual: Closest zoom of the establishing chain, before the journey fans out into eight planet scenes

content_blocks.scale: ~1.39 million km diameter (109x Earth's diameter); 99.86% of the Solar System's total mass
content_blocks.temperature: ~5,500 degrees C surface vs ~15 million degrees C core
content_blocks.power_source: Nuclear fusion — hydrogen fusing into helium
content_blocks.life_cycle: ~4.6 billion years old; ~10 billion year expected lifespan; will eventually become a red giant, then a white dwarf

interaction.visual: Surface/corona close-up with a subtle flare animation
interaction.branch_point: As this scene ends, an orbital path selector or simple 'continue' cue appears, launching the planet sequence
interaction.exit: Scroll pulls the camera outward and Mercury resolves into view

pages.name: Page 2, Scenes D-K — Planet template (build once, populate 8 times)

content_blocks_every_planet.hero: Full planet render, slow continuous rotation (40-60s per turn)
content_blocks_every_planet.quick_stat_strip: Distance from Sun, diameter, day length, year length, moon count (same four/five stats on every planet so they can be compared)
content_blocks_every_planet.overview_line: What it's made of — rocky / gas giant / ice giant
content_blocks_every_planet.qualitative_highlight: One-sentence 'why this planet is unique' fact, written not quoted from data
content_blocks_every_planet.deep_dive_panel: Atmosphere & surface temperature, notable moons, discovery date and exploring spacecraft/missions — collapsed by default behind a 'more' disclosure

interaction.reveal: Quick-stat strip appears first on arrival; deep-dive panel expands on continued scroll or tap/click
interaction.position_cue: Small orbital mini-map in a corner shows which planet is currently in view
interaction.nav: Prev/next arrows to jump directly between planets without re-scrolling the whole sequence

pages.name: Branch — The Earth-Moon System (optional detour)
pages.note: Not a stop on the main line. From the Earth scene the viewer can zoom further into the Earth-Moon pair before rejoining the main sequence at Mars. This is the deepest zoom level in the whole site.

content_blocks.formation: Giant impact hypothesis — ~4.5 billion years ago a Mars-sized protoplanet ('Theia') struck the young Earth at a glancing angle; debris flung into orbit coalesced into the Moon
content_blocks.physical_profile: Diameter ~3,476 km (about 27% of Earth's); mass ~1.2% of Earth's; surface gravity ~1.62 m/s^2 (about 16.6% of Earth's)
content_blocks.orbit_and_tidal_lock: Average distance ~384,400 km; tidally locked so the same face (~59% of the surface, counting libration) always points toward Earth
content_blocks.timekeeping: ~27.3-day sidereal orbit vs the ~29.5-day cycle of visible phases (new, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full) that people actually see from Earth
content_blocks.surface_and_environment: No atmosphere; heavily cratered highlands alongside dark basaltic 'maria' (ancient lava plains); temperatures swing from ~130 degrees C in direct sunlight to ~-180 degrees C in shadow; permanently shadowed polar craters hold water ice
content_blocks.effect_on_earth: Gravity drives ocean tides and helps stabilize Earth's axial tilt, keeping seasons regular over geologic time; the same geometry produces solar and lunar eclipses
content_blocks.slow_drift: Tidal forces are pushing the Moon away from Earth by about 3.8 cm per year
content_blocks.exploration: 6 crewed Apollo landings (1969-1972) put 12 people on the surface; current-era missions (Artemis, Chang'e, Chandrayaan, among others) target a return, with particular interest in the ice-bearing south pole

interaction.branch_trigger: A distinct 'zoom into the Moon' prompt on the Earth scene, visually separate from the prev/next planet arrows, so it reads as a detour rather than the next stop
interaction.on_entry: Camera pulls in on the Earth-Moon pair together, ideally at true relative size and distance, before easing into the Moon close-up
interaction.exit: A clear 'back to Earth' control returns the viewer to the Earth scene, which then continues normally to Mars — the branch must never be the only way forward

design_system.principle: The idea in one line: one planet, one screen, one column of text. The planet is the picture; the words sit beside it, never on top of it; the bottom rail answers the only navigation question a visitor has — 'where am I in the solar system?'
four_rules: The canvas stays quiet: deep space, faint stars, nothing that competes with the planet.
The planet owns the right side: same position and same optical size band on every planet page, so moving between planets feels like turning your head, not reloading a page.
Text is a single narrow column: hook first, numbers second, story third. Never more than one screen.
Progress is always visible: the orbit rail is the only persistent chrome on the page.

desktop.description: Planet vertically centred and positioned right; text column at left; orbit rail pinned to the bottom across the full width.
desktop.planet_diameter: 300-360px, centered on the right column, vertically middle-aligned to the canvas
desktop.text_column_width: max 44ch for hook and facts, 68ch absolute ceiling, left aligned, ragged right
desktop.clear_space: At least 64px between the text column and the planet's outer glow; at least 96px between content and the rail

mobile.description: Planet first (~190px), then planet name/hook/stats/facts stacked below, then the compressed orbit rail with labels only on the current stop.

layout.applies_to: Stage 4 planet pages define the canvas; Stages 1-3 (Milky Way, Solar System, Sun) inherit the same canvas, type system, and rail.

orbit_rail.concept: A miniature solar system, not a progress bar. Reads as distance travelled from the Sun.

anatomy.sun_anchor: Fixed at the far left, 16px, always lit — the origin of the journey
anatomy.orbit_line: 1px hairline at 14% opacity, running the full width of the content area
anatomy.filled_segment: The line from the Sun to the current planet, drawn in the solar gradient — this is the progress indicator
anatomy.stops: Eight dots spaced by a compressed (square-root) distance scale so Mercury-Mars don't bunch up at 3% of the width
anatomy.dot_size: Follows the planet's real diameter, compressed the same way: Mercury 7px up to Jupiter 16px — size carries information, don't flatten it

states.extras: Starlight hairline ring, soft glow in the planet's colour, label always on

orbit_rail.rule: Scale up rather than recolour — the highlight must survive on Mercury's grey as well as Neptune's blue. 1.55x is the smallest jump that reads instantly and still fits the 64px rail without shoving neighbours.
orbit_rail.timing: Transition is 350ms on a soft ease; the fill runs 500ms so the line arrives just after the dot settles.

color_tokens.rule: The planet tint appears in exactly four places: the orb body, its glow, the bullet marks in the fact list, and that planet's dot on the rail. Never as a background wash, never behind text.

typography.display_font: Bodoni Moda (engraved, high-contrast, like lettering on an old star atlas) — Google Font, fallback Georgia/Times New Roman/serif
typography.body_font: Spectral (built for reading on screen) — Google Font, fallback Georgia/Times New Roman/serif
typography.rule: Sentence case everywhere, including rail stop labels. Numbers always carry their unit and units are never abbreviated past recognition (e.g. '4,879 km', not '4879').

motion.planet_rotation: One slow continuous spin, 40-60s per turn — the only ambient motion on the page, and what makes the canvas feel alive
motion.stars: Static field, drawn once. A faint twinkle on a handful of stars is allowed; a moving parallax field is NOT allowed on planet pages — it fights the planet.
motion.planet_change: Outgoing orb fades and shrinks to 0.92, incoming orb fades up over 450ms; the rail dot grows at the same moment so both read as one action
motion.text: Fades in only, no slide. Staggered slide-ups on every block is the tell of a template — avoid it.
motion.reduced_motion: Honour prefers-reduced-motion: drop rotation and the fill animation, keep state changes instant

content_pattern_per_planet.hook: One sentence — the reason this planet is worth a screen. Written, not quoted verbatim from data.
content_pattern_per_planet.four_stats: Same four stats on every planet for comparability: distance from the Sun, diameter, day length, moons. Year length swaps in where the year is the interesting/strange part (Venus, Neptune).
content_pattern_per_planet.three_to_five_facts: One on composition, one on atmosphere or surface, one on what makes it unique, one on exploration — about twelve words each where possible.
content_pattern_per_planet.overflow_rule: Everything else from the research (mass, gravity, axial tilt, full mission histories) belongs behind a 'more' disclosure or a separate comparison view, not on the main canvas.

do: Keep the planet's centre at the same coordinates on every page
Let the glow bleed into the text gutter — it sells depth
Give the rail room; it needs 96px of empty canvas above it
Use the real size difference between dots — Jupiter should look like Jupiter
dont: Put text over the planet, or a panel behind the text
Add a second accent colour, a card, or a border-radius kit
Animate the starfield, the text and the planet all at once
Use the rail for anything but position in the journey — no percentages, no step counter
Shrink the current dot instead of growing it — the highlight is always the largest thing on the rail
accessibility_floor: Starlight-on-void contrast is about 15:1 — acceptable. Dust grey at 12px is the weakest pairing; never go below 13px with it on a coloured background.
Rail stops are <button> elements or links with a 44px tap target, an accessible name (e.g. 'Mars, planet 4 of 8'), and aria-current="page" on the active one
The highlight is carried by size, ring, and label — never by colour alone
Every orb/planet graphic has a text alternative; decorative starfield is aria-hidden

quantitative.orbital_speed: ~828,000 km/h (one orbit = ~230 million years, a 'galactic year')

qualitative: Classified as a barred spiral galaxy
Made of a central bulge, spiral arms, a surrounding halo, and dark matter
Contains gas, dust, and stellar nurseries where new stars form
Named 'Milky Way' from its milky band appearance in the night sky (Latin: Via Lactea)
Part of the 'Local Group' of galaxies, moving toward the Andromeda Galaxy (future collision predicted)

quantitative.asteroid_belt: over 1 million asteroids larger than 1 km

qualitative: Formed from a collapsing giant molecular cloud (nebular hypothesis)
Structure: inner rocky planets, asteroid belt, outer gas/ice giants, Kuiper Belt, Oort Cloud
Held together by the Sun's gravity
Planets orbit in roughly the same plane (ecliptic plane) and direction

quantitative.mass: 99.86% of the Solar System's total mass
quantitative.age: ~4.6 billion years; expected lifespan ~10 billion years

Powered by nuclear fusion (hydrogen fusing into helium)
Exhibits phenomena like sunspots, solar flares, and solar wind

planets.name: Mercury
planets.hook: Smallest planet; most extreme day/night temperature swing of any planet
planets.highlight: Smallest planet, extreme temperature swings, cratered like the Moon
planets.composition: Rocky terrestrial planet with a large metallic core (about 70% metal, 30% silicate rock).
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Virtually no atmosphere (only a thin exosphere); temperature swings from about -180°C at night to 430°C during the day — the most extreme swing of any planet.
planets.exploration: First visited by NASA's Mariner 10 (1974-75); explored in detail by MESSENGER (2011-2015); BepiColombo mission currently en route.
planets.unique_fact: It is the smallest and fastest-orbiting planet, heavily cratered, and experiences the most extreme temperature swings of any planet.

planets.name: Venus
planets.hook: Hottest planet due to a runaway greenhouse effect; rotates backward
planets.highlight: Hottest planet due to runaway greenhouse effect, rotates backward
planets.composition: Rocky terrestrial planet with a thick CO2 atmosphere and clouds of sulfuric acid.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Thick carbon dioxide atmosphere with clouds of sulfuric acid, causing a runaway greenhouse effect; surface averages about 465°C, the hottest of any planet.
planets.discovery: Known since antiquity as the 'morning/evening star'; first flown past by Mariner 2 (1962).
planets.exploration: Explored by the Soviet Venera program (first landing 1970), NASA's Magellan orbiter, and Japan's Akatsuki mission.
planets.unique_fact: It is the hottest planet despite not being closest to the Sun, and it uniquely rotates in the opposite direction to its orbit.

planets.name: Earth
planets.hook: The only known planet with life and liquid water on the surface
planets.highlight: Only known planet with life, liquid water, protective atmosphere
planets.composition: Rocky terrestrial planet with a layered structure: core, mantle, and crust.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere; average surface temperature about 15°C; liquid water covers roughly 71% of the surface.
planets.notable_moons: One moon: the Moon (see Earth-Moon branch for detail).
planets.discovery: Our home planet — studied continuously throughout human history.
planets.exploration: Explored extensively via satellites, the International Space Station, and countless Earth-observation missions.
planets.unique_fact: It is the only known planet to support life, protected by a magnetic field that shields it from harmful solar radiation.

planets.name: Mars
planets.hook: Iron-oxide dust gives it its red color; strong evidence of ancient water
planets.highlight: 'Red Planet' due to iron oxide dust, evidence of ancient water, target for human exploration
planets.composition: Rocky terrestrial planet with an iron-oxide-rich surface, giving it a reddish color.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Thin carbon dioxide atmosphere; average temperature around -63°C.
planets.notable_moons: Two small moons: Phobos and Deimos.
planets.discovery: Known since antiquity; first successfully flown past by Mariner 4 (1965).
planets.exploration: Explored by Viking landers, numerous orbiters, and rovers including Curiosity and Perseverance.
planets.unique_fact: Hosts the largest volcano in the Solar System (Olympus Mons) and shows strong evidence of ancient rivers and lakes.

planets.name: Jupiter
planets.hook: Largest planet; the Great Red Spot storm is bigger than Earth
planets.highlight: Largest planet, Great Red Spot storm, strong magnetic field
planets.composition: Gas giant composed mainly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Hydrogen/helium atmosphere featuring the Great Red Spot, a giant centuries-old storm, and distinct banded cloud patterns.
planets.notable_moons: 95 known moons, including the four large Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.
planets.discovery: Known since antiquity; Galileo Galilei discovered its four largest moons in 1610.
planets.exploration: Explored by Pioneer 10/11, Voyager 1 and 2, the Galileo orbiter, and the ongoing Juno mission.
planets.unique_fact: It is the largest planet, has the strongest planetary magnetic field, and even has a faint ring system.

planets.name: Saturn
planets.hook: Iconic ice-and-rock ring system; the only planet less dense than water
planets.highlight: Iconic ring system made of ice and rock, least dense planet (would float in water)
planets.composition: Gas giant composed mainly of hydrogen and helium.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Hydrogen/helium atmosphere; famous for its extensive, bright ring system made of ice and rock particles.
planets.notable_moons: 146 known moons, notably Titan (thick atmosphere, methane lakes) and Enceladus (icy geysers).
planets.discovery: Known since antiquity; rings correctly identified by Christiaan Huygens in 1655 after Galileo's earlier, unclear observations.
planets.exploration: Explored by Pioneer 11, Voyager 1 and 2, and extensively by the Cassini-Huygens mission (2004-2017).
planets.unique_fact: Its iconic rings make it instantly recognizable, and it is the least dense planet in the Solar System — it would float in water.

planets.name: Uranus
planets.hook: Rotates almost on its side (~98 degree tilt); pale blue-green from methane
planets.highlight: Rotates on its side (~98 degree tilt), pale blue-green from methane
planets.composition: Ice giant made of water, ammonia, and methane ices along with hydrogen and helium.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Hydrogen/helium/methane atmosphere giving it a pale blue-green color; extremely cold temperatures.
planets.notable_moons: 27 known moons, including Titania and Oberon.
planets.discovery: Discovered by William Herschel in 1781 — the first planet found using a telescope.
planets.exploration: Visited only once, by Voyager 2 during its 1986 flyby; no dedicated mission has been sent since.
planets.unique_fact: It rotates almost on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98°, likely the result of an ancient massive collision.

planets.name: Neptune
planets.hook: Fastest winds in the Solar System; found by math before it was observed
planets.highlight: Strongest winds in the Solar System, deep blue color, discovered through mathematical prediction
planets.composition: Ice giant with a composition similar to Uranus: water, ammonia, and methane ices plus hydrogen and helium.
planets.atmosphere_and_temperature: Hydrogen/helium/methane atmosphere; home to the strongest winds in the Solar System, reaching about 2,100 km/h.
planets.notable_moons: 14 known moons, notably Triton, which orbits in the opposite direction to Neptune's rotation.
planets.discovery: Discovered in 1846 by Johann Galle, based on calculations by Urbain Le Verrier predicting its position from Uranus's orbital irregularities.
planets.exploration: Visited only once, by Voyager 2 during its 1989 flyby; no dedicated mission has been sent since.
planets.unique_fact: Known for its deep blue color and for being the only planet discovered through mathematical prediction rather than direct observation.

content_data.data_freshness_note: Moon counts (especially for Jupiter and Saturn) update occasionally as new moons are confirmed — worth a quick check closer to launch/submission for precision.

ux_research_notes.scrollytelling_precedent: Many space-education sites use scrollytelling — scrolling triggers animations, zooms, or transitions — paired with parallax backgrounds to create a sense of depth and movement through space.
ux_research_notes.tooling: Three.js renders 3D scenes (rotating galaxy, planets) directly in the browser; GSAP's ScrollTrigger plugin ties animations and camera movement to scroll position for a smooth zoom-in narrative.
ux_research_notes.scale_comparison_technique: Real astronomical distances are too vast to represent literally on screen, so use relatable comparisons (e.g. 'if the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a peppercorn 30 meters away') or compressed, non-linear scale transitions to convey scale without making empty space feel boring.

project_name_rationale: The chosen name, 'The Galactic Canvas', reflects the site's core concept: presenting the vastness of the galaxy, the Solar System, and the planets as an unfolding visual and narrative canvas for the viewer to explore.

final_instruction: Build the complete site now, targeting Google AI Studio's app build mode. Implement Page 1 (cover) and Page 2 (the 11-scene scroll/zoom canvas: Milky Way, Solar System, Sun, then the 8 planets in order, plus the optional Earth-Moon branch) exactly per the information architecture. Apply the design system (colors, type, orbit rail, motion, do/don't, accessibility floor) exactly as specified. Populate every stat and fact from content_data verbatim, including each planet's composition, atmosphere_and_temperature, notable_moons, discovery, exploration, and unique_fact fields for the deep-dive disclosure panel, and the earth_moon_branch and ux_research_notes fields where relevant. Do not invent data not present in this spec; where creative copy is needed (hooks, transitions), keep it consistent in tone with the qualitative highlights given. Use Three.js + GSAP ScrollTrigger via CDN, no external image assets, and confirm the result renders and scrolls correctly inside AI Studio's preview.

instructions: Paste this entire JSON as the system/user prompt in a new AI Studio app (Build tab).

Prefer a single-file web app output (index.html with inline CSS/JS) so AI Studio can preview it immediately; if AI Studio's app scaffold uses separate files (e.g. index.html/index.css/index.tsx for a React+Vite template), keep the same content split across those files instead of forcing everything into one.
Load Three.js and GSAP + ScrollTrigger from a CDN (e.g. cdnjs or jsdelivr) via <script> tags — do not use npm imports unless AI Studio's template requires them.
Do not reference any local/relative image files; this spec intentionally avoids external image assets so the app works with zero uploaded media (procedural starfields and shaded-sphere planets only).
After generation, use AI Studio's preview to sanity-check scroll performance and the mobile breakpoint (<860px) before exporting or deploying.
